one_liner: Embeddable Rust per-topic write-ahead log engine; ~8% more unsynced writes/s than a local single-broker Kafka, tied when fsync'd.
what_it_does: walrus-rust is a crate linked into a Rust process that stores append-only, topic-named logs in preallocated files and returns entries through a per-topic read cursor, so it stands in for a local Kafka broker or a hand-rolled WAL inside one process, not for a Kafka cluster. The API is Walrus::new()/builder(), append_for_topic, batch_append_for_topic (atomic, up to 2,000 entries), and read_next/batch_read_for_topic with a checkpoint flag; the fsync policy (every N ms, SyncEach, NoFsync) and cursor persistence (StrictlyAtOnce or AtLeastOnce{persist_every}) are fixed when the instance is built. The repo now also ships distributed-walrus, a separate server with Raft-replicated metadata and its own length-prefixed text TCP protocol, which was not part of the benchmark.
how_it_is_fast: Each topic has one writer that puts a 256-byte rkyv-serialized header (length, owning topic, FNV-1a checksum) plus the payload into 10 MB blocks cut from sparse, preallocated 1 GB files with a single pwrite(). So the append path has no network hop, no wire protocol and, in NoFsync or Milliseconds mode, no fsync; a background thread deduplicates dirty files and fsyncs them as one io_uring batch every N ms. The newer batch_append_for_topic path submits up to 2,000 planned writes in one io_uring submission, but that path was not used in the Kafka comparison.
when_to_use: One Rust process needs a durable append-only log or queue per topic (event log, job queue, local WAL), and you would otherwise run a local Kafka broker just for that.
Many independent topics written from separate threads: writers are per topic and do not contend with each other (the benchmark used one topic per thread).
Throughput-first ingestion that can accept a bounded loss window (FsyncSchedule::Milliseconds, default 200 ms) or no durability at all; the measured edge over Kafka exists only in that unsynced mode.
Linux hosts that permit io_uring, if you plan to rely on the batch append/read APIs; the author says their non-io_uring fallback is roughly 5-10x slower.
Records of roughly 0.5 KB and up; every entry carries a fixed 256-byte header, so tiny records mostly write overhead.
when_not_to_use: You need Kafka semantics or ecosystem: wire/client compatibility, consumer groups, offset-based seek or replay, time-based retention. Walrus has one consumable cursor per topic and deletes a file once every block in it has been read. On HN the author said a Kafka translation layer was dropped because Walrus is message-based, not offset-based.
You need per-record durable throughput: with fsync on every write it measured 4,980 writes/s, a tie with Kafka (4,921) and behind RocksDB's WAL (5,222).
You have latency SLOs: no p50/p99 latency figures are published (a gap called out in the Show HN thread); only throughput was measured.

Linux sandboxes where io_uring_setup is blocked (AWS Fargate, Lambda, gVisor, restrictive seccomp). The background flush/cleanup thread panics at startup while Walrus::new() still returns Ok, so periodic fsync and file deletion silently stop (open issue #25).

Windows (does not compile; the maintainer said support is not planned, issue #26), or setups that need replicated data: the distributed mode's README describes Raft for metadata only, with each segment's data held by its leader node.

integration.form: crate (walrus-rust on crates.io; latest published release is 0.2.0 from 2025-10-19)
integration.dependencies: rand 0.8, memmap2 0.9, libc, rkyv 0.7 (validation), rkyv_derive, bytecheck 0.6, tracing; io-uring 0.7 on Linux only
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2024, so Rust 1.85+; no rust-version declared in Cargo.toml
integration.platforms: Linux primary (io_uring for batch I/O and background fsync; mmap backend as alternative); non-Linux Unix code paths exist without io_uring (not benchmarked); Windows does not compile
integration.thread_safety: Walrus is shared across threads behind Arc (the benchmark does this with 10 threads). Each topic's writer is guarded by mutexes, so appends to the same topic serialize. A single append, or a second batch, sent to a topic while a batch is in progress there returns ErrorKind::WouldBlock instead of waiting. Reader cursors sit behind a per-topic RwLock, and StrictlyAtOnce holds that lock across I/O.

gotchas: The fd backend throws away pwrite's result (`let _ = self.file.write_at(...)` in src/wal/storage.rs), and background fsync errors are only printed. So append_for_topic can return Ok after a failed or short write, for example on a full disk.

Debug output goes to stdout via println! on every append unless the WALRUS_QUIET env var is set. The benchmark sets WALRUS_QUIET=1, so production callers should too; even in quiet mode each check is an env-var lookup on the hot path.

Process-wide state leaks across instances. The fsync schedule that decides O_SYNC is a OnceLock set by the first Walrus created, and the fd/mmap backend choice is a global atomic. So the v0.2.0 post's pattern of several instances with different FsyncSchedules in one process does not give each instance its own file-open behavior. Also, SyncEach on the fd backend opens files O_SYNC and still calls fsync after every append.

Each entry costs a 256-byte header (docs/architecture.md still says 64 bytes). The header embeds the topic name and must serialize into 254 bytes, so very long topic names are rejected. The published MB/s figures count payload bytes only.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Walrus when you want a library inside a Rust process rather than a broker to operate; SMF's Seastar-based write-ahead log is the only sibling of similar shape. To replace Kafka as a networked, replicated service, Redpanda (Kafka-compatible, 12-70x lower p99.99 latency), Fluvio (~1.5x throughput) or Woodpecker (3.5x MB/s in local-FS mode) all claim larger margins than Walrus's ~8% unsynced edge.
verified_claims_summary: On unstated Linux hardware, 10 threads each wrote bursts of 500-1024-byte records to their own topic for a default 120 s: Walrus through its per-record pwrite() path averaged 1,205,762 unsynced writes/s, against 1,112,120 (~1.08x) for a Java producer (acks=all, idempotence, linger.ms=0) feeding one unreplicated Kafka broker on localhost:9092, and with fsync per write the result was 4,980 to 4,921 with RocksDB's WAL at 5,222. No CPU, disk, kernel, filesystem, Kafka version or broker flush setting is given, and the Kafka harness counts a record when send() enqueues it, not when the broker acknowledges it.
status_note: Active but effectively single-author (last commit 2026-05-13, MIT, ~1.9k stars) and small enough to vendor (~4.8k lines under src/), but crates.io still serves 0.2.0 from October 2025, so the WALRUS_DATA_DIR race fix (PR #22) and the ~13% write-throughput struct-packing change (PR #24) are git-only.
